name: Wendy Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Milking at six, sixty-odd goats on a rotary platform that turns slowly while you put the cups on. Then I'm in the dairy with Maren, who owns Larkspur, making the soft cheese, or turning the hard ones in the cave, which is really an old cold store. Afternoons depend on the season: hay in summer, raspberries and currants in July, fencing in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a school office for twenty-five years. When the school merged with another one, they cut the office staff and I took the deal. I'd always made cheese at home as a hobby, so I asked Maren if she'd take an apprentice who was older than her. She laughed and said she'd take anyone who turns up at six.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good and hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good part is making something you can hold. A school office never gives you a cheese at the end of the week. The hard part is my hands: I'm slow at the milking, and I still can't judge the curd by feel the way Maren does. So I write everything down and ask the AI things in the evenings, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a handy helper, not a revolution. I'd probably say it in the cheese-makers' online group, where we swap recipes, because half of them are excited about it and half are terrified. Somewhere in between is usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep using it the way I do. I ask it about acidity levels and starter cultures, I use it to keep our milk records tidy, it writes the labels. It's saved me hours. If it never gets bigger, I'm still glad of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning the cheese properly, maybe go on a two-day course on hard cheeses at the dairy college in spring. I'd help Maren put the milk records and orders on a simple system so she's not doing it at midnight. And we'd keep saving the usual, about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit relieved for the people who were scared, and a tiny bit bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a tiny bit bored. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like new things. I was the one at school who set up the parents' text messages and the online dinner money. Everyone grumbled for a term and then wondered how they lived without it. I'd miss having something to figure out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the farm do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Maren's careful. She'd keep the rotary parlour and the cave and carry on. Larkspur's not a big business, it's a good one, and that's enough for her.

S0.say: I'd say it's a handy helper, not a revolution, in the cheese-makers' online group where people are split between excitement and fear.
S0.think: She keeps using AI as she does now, for acidity levels, milk records and labels; it's saved her hours and she'd still be glad of it.
S0.do: Keeps learning the cheese, plans a two-day hard cheese course at the dairy college in spring, and helps Maren move milk records and orders onto a simple system. Keeps saving about 200 a month.
S0.feel: Calm, relieved for the worried ones, and a tiny bit bored.
S0.quote: Everyone grumbled for a term and then wondered how they lived without it.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is comfortable with technology and a bit disappointed by a plateau because she likes figuring things out. Her centre outlook shows as placing herself between the excited and the terrified. Making something you can hold is clearly what drew her to the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's worth learning now rather than complaining later, and I'd say it in the cheese group and to the other farm staff. I'd also say small farms will need help to keep up, because the kit isn't cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd see an opening. Maren hates the computer side, and I'm good at it. If machines take over the routine bits of milking and turning cheeses, someone needs to set them up and watch the numbers, and that could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at what's out there for small goat dairies, things like cameras that spot lame goats or a robot that turns the cheeses in the cave. I'd write Maren a proper plan with costs, nothing flashy. And I'd start teaching a cheese evening class at the village hall, for a bit of extra money and to keep my hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and interested. It's a puzzle I'd enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Larkspur who'd lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, the lad who does the turning in the cave three mornings a week. He's nineteen and it's his first job. I'd want Maren to move him onto something else, and I'd tell her that before any robot arrived. I'd hate to be the one who brought in the thing that sent him home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know what's worth buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask around and read a lot, and I'd ask the AI to compare them, then check with real farms. You don't buy kit off a brochure. I learned that from the school's photocopier.

S1.say: I'd say it's worth learning now rather than complaining later, and that small farms will need help to keep up because the kit isn't cheap.
S1.think: She sees an opening: Maren hates the computer side and Wendy is good at it, so she could set up and watch the new machines.
S1.do: Researches lameness cameras and cheese-turning robots for small goat dairies and writes Maren a plan with costs in the first year. Starts teaching a cheese evening class at the village hall for extra money.
S1.feel: Calm and interested, like a puzzle she'd enjoy.
S1.quote: I'd hate to be the one who brought in the thing that sent him home.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy's adaptability shows as a practical plan with costs, not enthusiasm for its own sake. Her concern for young Joe is a real check on her excitement. Her measure of whether kit works comes from long office experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and think about who gets the benefit, without throwing it all away. I'd say it in the cheese group and to our local councillor. People will need some kind of income while it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it rattles me. Two years is too short to build anything. I'd be sixty, the machines would do the milking and the turning and probably the cheese-making, and I'd have a few months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd learn every system Maren could trial in the first year, so I'm the one who runs them. In parallel I'd start a small hand-made cheese label, using Larkspur milk, selling at markets, and I'd put a couple of thousand of savings into a second-hand cheese vat. If it didn't pay in a year, I'd sell the vat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm the kind of person who adapts, but even I need some runway. Two years is a short runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people still pay for hand-made cheese in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, I think. People still buy hand-thrown mugs when factory ones are cheaper. A robot can milk a goat. I'm less sure anyone will pay extra for cheese a robot made. But it'd be a small market, and lots of people would have the same idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Graham say about spending the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham's a technician at the water company and he's careful with money. He'd say, Wendy, in a crisis you keep your cash. And he might be right. We'd argue, then we'd agree on a smaller vat.

S2.say: I'd say we need to slow down and think about who gets the benefit, without throwing it all away, and that people will need some income while it settles.
S2.think: It rattles her: two years is too short to build anything, she'd be 60, and machines might do the milking, turning and cheese-making.
S2.do: Learns every system Maren can trial in year one to become the one who runs them. Starts a small hand-made cheese label with Larkspur milk at markets, buying a second-hand vat with a couple of thousand from savings and selling it if it doesn't pay within a year.
S2.feel: Anxious, because even someone who adapts needs runway.
S2.quote: I'm the kind of person who adapts, but even I need some runway. Two years is a short runway.
S2.fieldNote: Wendy's instinct under pressure is to build something, but she admits the timeline undercuts it. The disagreement with her partner Graham about keeping cash is real and ends in compromise. She worries that many others would try the same hand-made route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make sensible plans, and I'd encourage other small farms to look at what they can do by hand that people will pay for. I'd say it at the market and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes it feel possible. I'd be sixty-three, and I could have a small cheese business running by then, alongside Larkspur. Even if the robots take the milking, I'd have something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the course on hard cheeses and start selling at two local markets. In year two I'd buy the vat and maybe a small press, around three thousand in total. And I'd help Maren bring in the robots in a way that keeps Joe and me on for the bits people still want done by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's like being given a proper deadline instead of a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. With two years I'm scrambling and spending in a panic. With five, I can test the market, see what sells, and only spend once I know. That's the difference between a hobby and a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham's health, maybe, or Maren selling up. And if every supermarket has robot-made cheese at half the price, the market might be smaller than I think. I'd keep my eyes open and not bet the house on it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to make sensible plans, and I'd encourage small farms to find what they can do by hand that people will pay for.
S3.think: Five years makes it feel possible: at 63 she could have a small cheese business of her own running alongside Larkspur.
S3.do: Takes the hard-cheese course and sells at two local markets in year one, then spends about three thousand on a vat and press in year two. Helps Maren bring in robots in a way that keeps her and Joe on for hand-made work.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited, like a proper deadline instead of a surprise.
S3.quote: That's the difference between a hobby and a business.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time changes Wendy's spending from panic to testing first, which she frames clearly. She names specific risks, Graham's health and Maren selling, without being thrown by them. Her plan still includes protecting Joe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's do it properly: train people, help small farms and make sure hand-made food has a place. I'd say it at the market and in the cheese group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. I'd be sixty-eight, probably winding down, and I'd have had ten years to build my cheese up. The robots would arrive just as I'm handing over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the cheese side slowly, learn whatever new machines Maren tries, and help her choose the ones that suit a small farm. I'd save for retirement and maybe train someone younger in the cheese, so it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about what it'll look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you train, if you could choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, if he wants it. He's got good hands and he listens. In ten years he could be running the cheese at Larkspur with a robot doing the heavy turning, and that's a decent life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji works in marketing and Emi's a physiotherapist. I'd tell Kenji to watch out, because the machines can write adverts already. Emi I'd worry about less. People will want a person's hands on their sore back for a long while yet.

S4.say: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's do it properly: train people, help small farms and make sure hand-made food has a place.
S4.think: It's mostly good for her: at 68 she'd be winding down after ten years building her cheese, with robots arriving as she hands over.
S4.do: Keeps building the cheese side slowly, learns the machines Maren tries and helps choose ones that suit a small farm. Saves for retirement and trains young Joe in the cheese-making.
S4.quote: In ten years he could be running the cheese at Larkspur with a robot doing the heavy turning, and that's a decent life.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Wendy turns to handing on her craft, choosing Joe as her successor. She sees robots and hand-made work living side by side. Her worry for her son Kenji's marketing job shows she knows where AI's reach is longest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to build anything, and I'd be sixty with a few months of savings. What would help is small start-up loans or grants for older people starting hand-made food businesses, and clear labels so customers can choose food made by people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what I'd want the machines to do. I'd want them to do the heavy lifting and the night checks, and leave us the bits we love. Nobody asks farmers that. They just sell us what they've made.

headlineQuote: A robot can milk a goat. I'm less sure anyone will pay extra for cheese a robot made.
portrait: Wendy Tanaka is 58, a former school office manager who has spent two and a half years as an apprentice at Larkspur, a goat dairy with cheese-making, hay and soft fruit. She's still behind on the hands-on skills but uses AI tools every day, for cheese recipes, milk records and planning, and she's curious and willing to take a sensible risk. She's pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, judging each change by whether it works rather than who's behind it. She stays calm through a plateau and steady change, seeing herself as the person who sets up the new machines, and is anxious with AGI in two years because there's no time to build anything of her own. With five or ten years she plans a small hand-made cheese business and sees the change as mostly an opportunity.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years is too short to build a hand-made cheese business or a new role, and she'd be 60 with a few months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Small start-up loans or grants for older workers launching hand-made food businesses, and clear labelling so customers can choose food made by people.
